sections.body: This field is about making quantitative research in AI and adjacent sciences repeatable, inspectable, and less dependent on tacit knowledge. AI is used to generate and check code, to translate plain language questions into database queries, to manage large scale compute on institutional data, and to simulate study designs before data collection. The work is not about replacing statistical judgment. It is about catching errors earlier, documenting steps, and letting a researcher rerun an analysis from raw data to final table.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are solved in practice. Notebooks, version control, and container images can make a pipeline reproducible when the original environment is captured. Plain language data questions work for well documented tables and simple aggregations, but they fail on ambiguous schemas, messy joins, and questions that require domain knowledge. Large scale compute on institutional data is often limited by access rules, data use agreements, and cost, not by model capability. Statistical code generated by AI can be useful for boilerplate, but it still needs tests, edge cases, and human review. The site has extracted 11,795 claims from research works, which makes the question of whether those claims can be reproduced a practical one.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The page on Reproducible Notebooks and Pipelines is the foundation, because it covers how to capture an analysis so another person can run it. Asking Data Questions in Plain Language extends that foundation to interfaces that turn a question into a query, with all the caveats about schema and intent. Large Scale Compute on Institutional Data addresses the infrastructure and governance side, where compute meets restricted datasets. Writing Statistical Code with AI focuses on the code layer, including tests and review practices for generated analysis code. Testing a Study Design Before Data Collection sits earlier in the timeline, using simulation to check whether a planned study can answer its question before any data is gathered. Together these pages move from setup to query to compute to code to design, and a reader can enter at the point that matches their current bottleneck.
